title: Seeing, not swept
hook: the last discourse: training the senses is not closing the eyes but seeing without being swept away

segments.voice: Yesterday: pindapata, Sariputta's bright face, and your line, review the road. What rose on the way when you walked it back? Today, the last of the hundred and fifty-two. Day five hundred seventeen.

The last discourse in the Middle-Length Sayings opens with a short, slightly awkward conversation. The Buddha is staying at Kajangala, and a young brahmin named Uttara comes to visit. He's a student of a teacher called Parasariya. Does your teacher teach the development of the senses? the Buddha asks. Yes, says Uttara. How? Like this: you don't see forms with the eye, and you don't hear sounds with the ear. Then, the Buddha says, a blind person and a deaf person must be very developed indeed. Today: seeing, not swept.
screen: `THE LAST DISCOURSE.` → `UTTARA'S TEACHER: DON'T SEE.` → `THEN THE BLIND ARE DEVELOPED?`

segments.voice: Uttara goes quiet. The text says he sat silent, shoulders drooping, head down, with nothing to say. The Buddha doesn't press him. He turns to Ananda and teaches the other way, the development of the senses in his own discipline. When someone sees a form with the eye, something agreeable arises, or disagreeable, or both. That's going to happen. Eyes see. The trained person understands: this has arisen in me. It's conditioned, it's coarse, it's dependently arisen. But there's something peaceful and fine: equanimity. Then the reaction fades, and equanimity remains. The pictures are about speed. For the eye, as quickly as someone with good sight might open and shut their eyes. For the ear, as quickly as a strong man snaps his fingers. For the nose, like raindrops rolling off a sloping lotus leaf without sticking. For the tongue, like spitting out a bit of saliva gathered on the tip of the tongue. For the body, like a strong man straightening a bent arm. For the mind, like two or three drops of water falling on an iron pan heated all day: they vanish almost at once. The Pali word for the senses here is indriya, the faculties. So the last discourse of the whole collection lands on something modest. Training isn't shutting the senses down. Liking and disliking will still arise. The skill is in what happens next: seeing it, and letting it go before it carries you off. The eyes stay open. You see, and you stay.
screen: `UTTARA, SILENT, SHOULDERS DOWN` · `THIS HAS ARISEN IN ME` · `A BLINK, A SNAP, A DROP ON IRON` · `EYES OPEN, NOT CARRIED OFF` · then, large: `SEE AND STAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see without being swept. Let your gaze rest, eyes open and soft, on whatever is in front of you. When a liking or a disliking rises, a little pull or push, notice it: this has arisen. Then let it fall away, like water on a hot pan. Back to just seeing. If a thought drags you off, that's fine. Open and shut your eyes once, and begin again. The bell holds the time.
Seeing. Not closing the eyes, but seeing what arises, liking or disliking, and letting it settle into equanimity before it sweeps you away. Today's word.
Your line: see and stay. Today, when something you dislike comes into view, keep looking, notice the push, and let it pass like a blink. Day five hundred seventeen.

screen: `DAY 517 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: LOOKING BACK: THE GOOD POTTER.`

howItsDone: Buddhist meditators in several schools practice open-eyed awareness and sense restraint in daily life: noticing liking and disliking as they arise and returning to equanimity, rather than avoiding the world.

myth: in MN 152 the Buddha says real training means not seeing or hearing
that was Uttara's teacher's view; the Buddha says then the blind and deaf would be developed.
MN 152 is the last discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings
the collection ends with the development of the senses.
the trained person never feels liking or disliking
they still arise. the skill is seeing them and letting them settle quickly.

fork.setup: the Buddha has just answered Uttara: then the blind and the deaf must be developed. Uttara has no reply. what does the Buddha do?
options: turns to Ananda and teaches the other way.
presses Uttara until he admits he's wrong.
sends Uttara back to his teacher with a message.
fork.reveal: he lets the silence stand and teaches Ananda the noble development of the senses, with Uttara still sitting there to hear it.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit indriya: faculty, sense power. MN 152 is about developing all six.

trapdoor: what you thought: training the senses means shutting them down.
what it means: seeing what arises, liking or disliking, and letting it settle into equanimity, quickly.

what a scholar hears: the Indriyabhavana Sutta closes the Majjhima with a graded teaching (the noble development, the learner, the noble one) and six similes whose common thread is the speed of letting go.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 152, Indriyabhavana Sutta (the development of the faculties)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the indriya-as-'ruling' etymology from the teach and the original note; smoothed a doubled 'And... And' sentence; practice opening changed so it doesn't echo day 512's.
MN 152 paraphrased. Confirm the setting (Kajangala, the Mukhelu or Suvelu grove), the name of Uttara's teacher (Parasariya / Parasiriya), and Uttara's silent, drooping posture.

Confirm the six similes and their assignment to senses (eye: opening and shutting the eyes; ear: snapping fingers; nose: drops on a lotus leaf; tongue: spitting saliva; body: extending a bent arm; mind: drops on a heated iron pan).
The gloss of indriya as related to 'ruling' (Indra) is common in traditional explanations; confirm or remove.
